common_name: Unique Hydrangea (Vigorous Very Large White Panicle Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Unique is a vigorous panicle hydrangea bearing some of the largest flower panicles in the species.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Unique produces very large, dense, cone-shaped white flower panicles on a vigorous, large-growing shrub, among the biggest blooms and biggest overall plants in the panicle hydrangea group, making it a substantial specimen or informal screen where its eventual size can be accommodated. Like other panicle hydrangeas it blooms reliably on new growth regardless of soil pH, so flower color never shifts. Prune in late winter to shape and control size, cutting back last year's growth by about a third to encourage strong new flowering stems.

common_name: Kyushu Hydrangea (Upright Glossy-Leaved White Panicle Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Kyushu bears glossy foliage and an upright habit distinct from many looser panicle hydrangea cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Kyushu bears creamy white, conical flower panicles with a light fragrance on an upright, vigorous shrub with notably glossy, dark green foliage, a tidier and more polished look than many looser-habited panicle hydrangea cultivars. Its strong upright growth also makes it adaptable for training as a small standard tree form. Prune in late winter to shape and control size, cutting back last year's growth by about a third to encourage strong new flowering stems.

common_name: Pink Diamond Hydrangea (White Panicles Aging to Pink)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Diamond is an RHS Award of Garden Merit panicle hydrangea whose white flowers age to deep pink.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Pink Diamond opens large, conical white flower panicles that gradually deepen to a rich pink as they age through late summer into fall, so a single plant shows both colors at once, a color-change trait shared by several panicle hydrangea cultivars and recognized with a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit. It grows into a large, vigorous shrub or small tree form over time. Prune in late winter to shape and control size, cutting back last year's growth by about a third to encourage strong new flowering stems.

common_name: Vanille Fraise Hydrangea (Bicolor White-to-Strawberry-Red Panicle Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Vanille Fraise is a French-bred panicle hydrangea whose panicles shift from white to strawberry-red as they age.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Vanille Fraise opens creamy white flower panicles at the base that shift dramatically to a deep strawberry-red toward the tip as the season progresses, so a single panicle displays a striking gradient of color, a French-bred introduction that has become one of the most popular bicolor panicle hydrangea cultivars. Its sturdy stems hold the heavy panicles upright well through wind and rain. Prune in late winter to shape and control size, cutting back last year's growth by about a third to encourage strong new flowering stems.

common_name: Hayes Starburst Hydrangea (Double Star-Shaped White Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Hayes Starburst is a smooth hydrangea selection with unusual fully double, star-shaped florets.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade. Hayes Starburst bears rounded flower heads made up of unusual double, star-shaped white florets, a distinctive texture unlike the simpler flat-petaled florets of typical smooth hydrangea cultivars like Annabelle. Like other Hydrangea arborescens selections it blooms reliably on new growth each year, so flower color and bloom performance don't depend on winter bud survival the way old-wood mophead types do, and cold winters that damage other hydrangeas won't affect its bloom. Cut stems back hard, to 12-18 inches, in late winter to encourage a fresh flush of sturdy flowering stems.

common_name: White Dome Hydrangea (Lacecap Flat-Headed Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; White Dome is a lacecap-form smooth hydrangea, an airier alternative to the rounded mophead form of Annabelle.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade. White Dome bears large, flat, lacecap-form flower heads with showy sterile white florets ringing a center of smaller fertile flowers, a more open, naturalistic look and much better resistance to flopping in rain than the heavy round mophead form of Annabelle-type smooth hydrangeas. It blooms reliably on new growth each year regardless of winter cold, so bloom performance isn't at risk from bud damage. Cut stems back hard, to 12-18 inches, in late winter to encourage a fresh flush of sturdy flowering stems.

common_name: Grandiflora Hydrangea (Hills of Snow, Historic Round White Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Grandiflora, known historically as Hills of Snow, is an older round-flowered smooth hydrangea selection predating Annabelle.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade. Grandiflora, long known by the common name Hills of Snow, was one of the earliest selections of smooth hydrangea bred for large, rounded, all-sterile-floret flower heads, predating the now more famous Annabelle by several decades and helping establish the mophead-form smooth hydrangea as a garden staple. It blooms reliably on new growth each year regardless of winter cold. Cut stems back hard, to 12-18 inches, in late winter to encourage a fresh flush of sturdy flowering stems, since older, thinner stems tend to flop under the flower weight.

common_name: Harmony Oakleaf Hydrangea (Very Large Double Panicle Oakleaf Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Harmony bears exceptionally large, heavy, fully double flower panicles that often cause branches to arch or weep under their weight.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade. Harmony bears some of the largest and most densely doubled flower panicles of any oakleaf hydrangea cultivar, so heavy that mature branches often arch gracefully or weep under the sheer weight of bloom, creating a dramatic, fountain-like effect in early summer, with the classic oak-shaped leaves turning burgundy-red in fall. Its bold flower display makes it a strong specimen shrub, though it needs more room to display its arching form than compact oakleaf cultivars. Prune only immediately after flowering to shape, since it blooms on old wood and later pruning removes next year's flowers.

common_name: Preziosa Mountain Hydrangea (Mophead Aging Pink to Deep Rose)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Preziosa is a compact mountain hydrangea whose mophead blooms age from pink to a deep rose-red.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Preziosa is a compact mountain hydrangea, a smaller, more shade- and heat-tolerant relative of bigleaf hydrangea from the mountains of Korea and Japan, bearing rounded mophead flower clusters that open pink and deepen through the season to a rich rose-red, a color progression more dramatic than most macrophylla cultivars show. Its modest size makes it more practical than bigleaf hydrangea in smaller gardens, and it flowers reliably even in warm-climate gardens where H. macrophylla can struggle. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to shape.

common_name: Miyama Yae Murasaki Hydrangea (Double Purple-Blue Lacecap Mountain Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Miyama Yae Murasaki bears unusual fully double, purple-blue lacecap florets.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Miyama Yae Murasaki, whose Japanese name translates roughly to "deep mountain double purple," bears lacecap flower heads in which even the outer sterile florets are fully double, a refined, layered texture rare among hydrangeas, opening in rich purple-blue that shifts with soil pH like other mountain and bigleaf hydrangea types. This compact, shade- and heat-tolerant mountain hydrangea performs reliably in warm-climate gardens where straight bigleaf hydrangea can struggle. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to shape.

common_name: Kiyosumi Mountain Hydrangea (Red-Purple Edged Lacecap with Reddish New Growth)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Kiyosumi emerges with reddish new foliage and bears lacecap flowers edged in red-purple.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Kiyosumi emerges each spring with new foliage flushed reddish-bronze before maturing green edged in maroon, and bears lacecap flower heads whose white to pale sepals are distinctly rimmed in red-purple, giving the plant multi-season interest beyond its summer bloom. This compact, shade- and heat-tolerant mountain hydrangea performs reliably in warm-climate gardens where straight bigleaf hydrangea can struggle. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to shape.

common_name: Shirofuji Mountain Hydrangea (Double White Lacecap Mountain Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Shirofuji bears unusually double white lacecap florets.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Shirofuji bears lacecap flower heads in which the outer sterile florets are fully double, layered like tiny white pompoms ringing the smaller central fertile flowers, an elegant, refined texture among mountain hydrangea cultivars. This compact, shade- and heat-tolerant type performs reliably in warm-climate gardens where straight bigleaf hydrangea can struggle. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to shape.

common_name: Beni-Gaku Mountain Hydrangea (Lacecap Turning Crimson in Sun and Fall)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Beni-gaku ('crimson picture frame') is a mountain hydrangea whose lacecap flowers deepen to crimson-red in sun and fall.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Beni-gaku, whose Japanese name means roughly "crimson picture frame," bears lacecap flower heads that open blue or pink and deepen dramatically to rich crimson-red with more sun exposure and as the season progresses into fall, framing the flower head like its namesake. This compact, shade- and heat-tolerant mountain hydrangea performs reliably in warm-climate gardens where straight bigleaf hydrangea can struggle. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to shape.

common_name: Miranda Climbing Hydrangea (Gold-Variegated Foliage Climbing Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade against a wall, fence, or sturdy tree; Miranda is a gold-variegated selection of climbing hydrangea, a slow-establishing but eventually vigorous self-clinging vine.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade against a wall, fence, or sturdy tree trunk the vine can cling to with its aerial rootlets. Miranda bears the same white lacecap flowers and peeling cinnamon bark as the species climbing hydrangea, but with leaves broadly edged in gold that brighten a shady wall even out of bloom. Like other climbing hydrangeas it establishes slowly for the first several years before growing vigorously once rooted in, eventually reaching great heights on a sturdy support. Prune after flowering only to control size or remove wayward growth, since it needs minimal routine pruning once established.

common_name: Firefly Climbing Hydrangea (Gold-Edged Variegated Foliage Climbing Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade against a wall, fence, or sturdy tree; Firefly is a gold-edged variegated selection of climbing hydrangea.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade against a wall, fence, or sturdy tree trunk the vine can cling to with its aerial rootlets. Firefly bears the same white lacecap flowers and peeling cinnamon bark as the species climbing hydrangea, with leaves edged in bright gold that catch the light against a shaded wall or fence even when the plant isn't in bloom. Like other climbing hydrangeas it establishes slowly for the first several years before growing vigorously once rooted in. Prune after flowering only to control size or remove wayward growth, since it needs minimal routine pruning once established.
